clinician.trajectory_summary: A 49-year-old male presented with a 3-day history of severe frontal-to-occipital headache, photophobia, nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea, with normothermia, normal vital signs, and preserved consciousness (GCS 15). MRI on admission revealed a haemorrhagic sellar mass. During hospitalization, polyuria of up to 12 L/day was documented. Copeptin levels during thirsting (4.3 pmol/L at t0 and 4.2 pmol/L at t7) were inappropriately low, and the patient demonstrated a robust response to desmopressin treatment, confirming central diabetes insipidus (CDI). Polyuria normalized with desmopressin treatment after day 5 of admission. The acute meningeal symptoms (headache, photophobia, nausea, vomiting) represent hypernatremia-induced neurological manifestations secondary to unrecognized CDI with severe polyuria caused by the haemorrhagic sellar mass damaging the hypothalamic-pituitary axis. The patient was discharged on desmopressin 10 μg twice daily along with L-thyroxine 100 μg/day, hydrocortisone 15-10-0 mg, and testosterone depot 250 mg, indicating multiple pituitary hormone deficiencies from the sellar mass.

final.trajectory_summary: A 49-year-old male presented with a 3-day history of severe frontal-to-occipital headache, photophobia, nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea, with normothermia, normal vital signs, and preserved consciousness (GCS 15). MRI on admission revealed a haemorrhagic sellar mass. During hospitalization, polyuria of up to 12 L/day was documented. Copeptin levels during thirsting (4.3 pmol/L at t0 and 4.2 pmol/L at t7) were inappropriately low, and the patient demonstrated a robust response to desmopressin treatment, confirming central diabetes insipidus (CDI). Polyuria normalized with desmopressin treatment after day 5 of admission. The acute meningeal symptoms (headache, photophobia, nausea, vomiting) represent hypernatremia-induced neurological manifestations secondary to unrecognized CDI with severe polyuria caused by the haemorrhagic sellar mass damaging the hypothalamic-pituitary axis. The patient was discharged on desmopressin 10 μg twice daily along with L-thyroxine 100 μg/day, hydrocortisone 15-10-0 mg, and testosterone depot 250 mg, indicating multiple pituitary hormone deficiencies from the sellar mass.

key_supporting_evidence.claim: Patient presented with acute meningeal symptoms (severe frontal-to-occipital headache, photophobia, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea) over 3 days with normothermia, normal vital signs, and GCS 15
MRI on admission revealed a haemorrhagic sellar mass
Polyuria of up to 12 L/day was documented during hospitalization
Copeptin levels during thirsting were inappropriately low (4.3 pmol/L at t0 and 4.2 pmol/L at t7), indicating inadequate vasopressin response
Central diabetes insipidus was diagnosed based on copeptin levels and robust response to desmopressin treatment
Polyuria normalized with desmopressin treatment after day 5 of admission
Patient was discharged on desmopressin 10 μg bid, L-thyroxine 100 μg/day, hydrocortisone 15-10-0 mg, and testosterone depot 250 mg, indicating multiple pituitary hormone deficiencies

ruled_out_or_less_likely_alternatives.basis: Normothermia, normal vital signs, and preserved consciousness at presentation; no CSF analysis reported showing inflammatory changes; acute meningeal symptoms resolved with desmopressin treatment and correction of hypernatremia, not with antimicrobial therapy

ruled_out_or_less_likely_alternatives.alternative: Primary polydipsia or nephrogenic diabetes insipidus
ruled_out_or_less_likely_alternatives.basis: Copeptin levels during thirsting were inappropriately low (4.3-4.2 pmol/L), confirming central (vasopressin-deficient) rather than nephrogenic or primary polydipsic etiology; robust response to desmopressin confirms central CDI

remaining_uncertainties: Serum sodium and osmolality at admission not documented; hypernatremia as the mechanism for acute neurological symptoms is inferred but not directly confirmed
Urine osmolality during acute illness not reported; low urine osmolality characteristic of CDI is inferred from polyuria and desmopressin responsiveness but not directly measured
Pathology or histology of the haemorrhagic sellar mass not reported; underlying etiology of the sellar mass (e.g., pituitary adenoma, craniopharyngioma, hemorrhagic infarction) remains unspecified
CSF analysis not performed or reported; meningeal irritation from the haemorrhagic mass versus pure metabolic etiology of meningeal symptoms not definitively distinguished
Exact timing of desmopressin initiation and precise timeline of acute symptom resolution not explicitly documented
